_readme.covers: Progression quality for chord types introduced in Units 6-10: I6, V6, VII6, V7 inversions, IV/II/II6 as intermediates, the cadential 6/4, and deceptive resolutions of seventh chords.
_readme.structure: Each rule has: id, quality, from, to, feedback.

matching.from: Root numerals for the previous chord. Empty list = applies only to the very first chord.
matching.to: Root numerals for the current chord.
matching.bare_root: A bare numeral like 'V' matches any inversion of V.
matching.figured: A numeral with a figure like 'V65' matches only that inversion.

how_to_add_a_rule: 1. Copy a rule block between { and }.
2. Give it a new unique id.
3. Set from and to as above.
4. Pick a quality: excellent, good, fair, discouraged, bad.
6. Save. No trailing comma after the last rule.

rules.feedback: Root-position V7 to I. The leading tone rises to 1, the seventh falls to 3, and the bass steps to the tonic. The strongest possible authentic close.
V6/5 to I. Bass is the leading tone, which rises to 1 while the chordal seventh falls. The most forceful inversion of V7 at a close.
V4/3 to I6. Bass 2 falls to 3 in first inversion and the seventh also descends. Both tendency tones resolve correctly.
V4/2 to I6. The bass is the chordal seventh, which must fall by step, so it lands on I6. This is the only idiomatic resolution for V4/2.
V7 to vi. A deceptive resolution. The seventh still resolves down, but the other voices slide into vi instead of I, avoiding closure.
V4/3 to vi. Less common than V7 to vi because the extra seventh makes the deceptive effect stronger than the ear expects.
V4/2 to vi. The seventh in the bass must resolve down by step, so if it does go to vi it lands awkwardly. Avoid this combination.
V7 to I6. The resolution of the seventh (4-3) combined with the bass motion 5-3 creates bad hidden octaves. Use V5/3 or V6 instead.
I6 to V6 as a neighboring motion. Bass steps 3 to 7 and returns. Idiomatic expansion of tonic within a phrase.
I6 to vi. Bass 3 to 6 is a descending third. Idiomatic expansion of tonic into the submediant area.
I6 to the cadential 6/4. The bass steps 3 to 5, preparing the cadential suspension.
V6 to I. Bass 7 rises to 1. One of the smoothest ways to close a phrase without the weight of root-position V.
V6 to vi. A deceptive resolution in first inversion. The bass steps 7 to 1 while the upper voices avoid the tonic triad.
V6 to root-position V. Bass moves 7 to 5. Clear harmonic arrival after the contrapuntal first-inversion stage.
V6 to subdominant. The leading tone in the bass must continue by step to I. Going backward to a predominant leaves it unresolved.
I6 to IV. Bass moves 3 to 6, giving a smooth stepwise ascent that keeps the harmony moving forward.
I6 to ii (or ii6). Bass 3 to 4 is a step upward. The predominant first inversion leads cleanly into the cadence.
I6 to V. Bass 3 to 5 is a skip of a third, which is fine because the chords are in different functions.
I6 to vii°6. Bass 3 to 2 opens a stepwise descent back to I. Contrapuntal expansion of tonic.
vii°6 to I. In first inversion the leading tone sits in the bass and resolves up to the tonic. Textbook contrapuntal close.
vii°6 to I6. 4 is allowed to ascend to 5 (parallel 10ths above the bass), which produces a fluent stepwise motion.
vii°6 to V. The leading tone in the bass must rise, but V requires it to stay or fall. This clash is why vii°6 rarely resolves to V.
I to vii°6. A passing chord that opens a stepwise bass line 1-2-3. Prepares the return to I6.
vii°6 to vi. The leading tone in the bass resolves up to the tonic of vi. Deceptive flavour, less common than vii°6 to I.
Subdominant to dominant. Root motion by step but with the pull of a 5th underneath. The classic pre-cadential preparation.
IV6 to V. Bass 6 to 5 is a descending step — the smoothest approach to a cadence. In minor this is the Phrygian cadence.
IV6 to I. The bass leaps down a sixth, giving a disjunct effect. Acceptable, but IV or IV6 to V is usually stronger.
ii6 to V. Bass 4 to 5 is a step upward into the dominant. Characteristic of Mozart, Haydn, and Beethoven at cadences.
Supertonic to dominant. Another step down the circle of fifths. Combined with V to I, this is the fundamental cadential chain.
ii6/5 to V. Bass 4 steps up to 5 and the seventh resolves down, giving a smooth cadential approach.
ii4/3 to V6. Bass 6 falls to 7 (leading tone) and the seventh resolves down. Smooth first-inversion dominant.
ii4/2 to V6. The bass is the chordal seventh of ii, which falls by step. V6 is the only idiomatic resolution.
ii7 to V. Bass 2 to 5 is a fourth, so the chord progresses by the circle of fifths. Strong pull into the dominant.
IV7 to V. The subdominant seventh intensifies the approach to the dominant. Watch for parallel fifths; the standard fix is to leap the alto.
Supertonic seventh chord moving to the tonic. The seventh should resolve down by step to V, not skip to I. This weakens the cadential pull.
IV6 to ii6. Both chords share subdominant function, so the motion feels redundant rather than progressive.
ii6 to subdominant. Both chords share subdominant function, so the direction feels redundant. The subdominant usually precedes the supertonic, not the reverse.
I6 to ii6. Bass 3 to 4 is a step. Idiomatic stepwise approach to the cadential ii6.
IV to ii6. The 5-6 technique: the subdominant's fifth rises to the sixth above a stationary bass. Idiomatic.
Approaching the cadential 6/4 from tonic. The bass steps to 5 while the upper voices embellish. Standard preparation.
IV to the cadential 6/4. The subdominant's 4th is held over as the 4th of the 6/4, preparing the suspended dissonance.
ii6 to the cadential 6/4. The bass 4 to 5 supports the acceleration toward V.
ii to the cadential 6/4. Bass 2 to 5 is a fourth. Prepares the cadence less smoothly than ii6.
The cadential 6/4 resolves to V. This is the only resolution that respects the chord's true function — an intensification of the dominant.
Cadential 6/4 to V4/2. A mid-phrase delay of the cadence — the bass steps down while the dissonance is held over.
Cadential 6/4 resolving directly to I. The chord is not a tonic, so treating it as one leaves the dominant's tension unresolved.
Cadential 6/4 to first-inversion tonic. The bass keeps moving but the cadence is weakened. Rarely used.
Cadential 6/4 moving to subdominant. Neither chord is heard as a stable point; the 6/4's function is contradicted.
A cadential 6/4 must resolve to V or V4/2. Any other resolution contradicts its function as an intensified dominant.
IV to IV7. The added seventh is prepared as a common tone from IV. Watch for parallels when moving on to V.
Tonic to ii7 (or ii6/5). The seventh enters as a common tone or a stepwise descent, preparing the dissonance.
Approaching V7 from a predominant. The 4 held over becomes the seventh of V7 — the strongest possible preparation for the dominant.
Tonic to V6/5. The seventh enters by common tone or stepwise motion, preparing the leading-tone bass.
V6 to a predominant. The bass of V6 (the leading tone) must continue by step to I or I6. Going backward leaves the leading tone unresolved.
V6/5 to a predominant. The bass must ascend to 1 and the seventh must resolve down. Any other target leaves both tendency tones unsatisfied.
V4/2 to anything but I6. The bass is the chordal seventh and must fall by step. Only I6 continues the resolution correctly.
V4/3 to a non-tonic chord. The seventh should resolve down to 3 of I, or ascend to 5 in parallel 10ths into I6.
vii°6 to a non-tonic chord. The leading tone in the bass wants to rise to 1. Going elsewhere inverts the natural resolution.
